description: People mapping (Phase 4a, settled by Ben 2026-10-28). One row per source term: the people value that peoples_regions[].people, names[].peoples and native[].people take for it. draft-v2.1 applies the table and flags any term not in it; verify-v2.1 checks against it and refuses an unlisted term; the validator rejects a people value outside the set of `people` values below. `pilot` says how the ten pilot entries' existing flags would change under this table; the pilot entries are not re-run or edited.

rows.term: Russian, Russians, Russian peasants, Russia, Russia's, русскій, русская, русское, русскіе, русскія, русскаго, русской, русскому, русскомъ, русскую, русскою, русскихъ, русскимъ, русскими, Россіи, Россіей, Россійской, Россійскомъ, россіяне
rows.reasoning: The sources name the people directly. Where a page says only "the peasants" inside a passage about Russia (Ralston's Russian peasants), the context fixes Russians, as draft-v2 already ruled.
rows.note: The context rule is the narrowest reading; it is not used to file a named Little-Russian or White-Russian region as Russian. "Russia" and "Россіи" can name the whole Empire, which took in Little-Russia and White-Russia, and Afanasyev's "русскій" sometimes covers all the East Slavs: a row rests on these forms only where the passage names no other people, and the entry's region keeps the source's word.
rows.pilot: No change. Rows filed this way in all ten pilot entries stand.

rows.reasoning: Machal prints "Siberian Russians" (p.268); Afanasyev's southern Siberia sits in the same Russian-language tradition.
rows.note: Siberia also has non-Slavic peoples; the row covers only the Russian settlers the pages describe.
rows.pilot: No change (poludnitsa rows 10-11).

rows.reasoning: Afanasyev writes as a Russian for Russian readers, so "among us" is read as Russians when no other people is named in the sentence.
rows.note: On p.557 the same passage says the belief survives chiefly in the Ukraine and White Russia, so a reader may take "among us" to mean Ukrainians and Belarusians there.
rows.pilot: vampir /names/primary/native/1: the flag stands; the reading is now the table's, but the row is contested, so the flag is kept for the reader.

rows.reasoning: Little-Russia is the 19th-century name for the Ukrainian lands of the Russian Empire, and the sources use it for the people Ralston also calls Little-Russians. The region text keeps the source's word.
rows.note: The name itself is an imperial usage some readers object to; it appears only as the source's region text, never as the people.
rows.pilot: leshy /peoples_regions/6: the flag (a translation choice the page does not confirm) is cleared by the table. rusalka /peoples_regions/4 and vodyanoi /peoples_regions/7 are unchanged.

rows.term: Little-Russians, Little Russians, Little-Russian, малорусскій, малор., малорусская, малороссійскихъ, малороссы, малороссамъ, Малороссіяне, малоруссы, малоруссовъ, малоруссами, малорусской, малорусскому, малорусскомъ, малорусскою, малорусскую, малорусскихъ, малорусскимъ, малорусскіе, малорусскія, малорусское, малороссійская, малороссійской, малороссійскомъ, малороссійскимъ, малороссійскаго, малороссійское, малороссійскіе
rows.reasoning: The older English and Russian name for Ukrainians; Machal uses it beside "Ukranians" for the same people. Ralston prints the adjective "a Little-Russian variant" (1873 p.181) and Afanasyev "малорусскій варіантъ" (1868 p.699) for the same tale. Afanasyev abbreviates the adjective as "малор." in a list of word forms ("Волкодлакъ (малор. вовкулакъ, вовкунъ, бѣлор. вавкалакъ", 1869 p.527), and has "малорусская сказка" (1869 p.392) and "Въ пѣсняхъ малороссійскихъ" (1869 p.394).
rows.note: As for Little-Russia: the word stays in region text, the people is Ukrainians.
rows.pilot: No v2 flag. The Phase 1 flags on it (domovoi, baba-yaga) would be cleared.

rows.reasoning: Ralston labels forms "South-Russian" in the same way he labels others "Little-Russian", for the speech of the Ukrainian governments. Ralston 1873 p.178 has "a proverb common to Poland and South Russia", the same usage as a place name.
rows.note: "South-Russian" is not stated to equal Little-Russian on p.410, and in other usage it can cover the Don and New Russia, which were not only Ukrainian.
rows.pilot: vampir /names/variants/1: the flag (an interpretation not stated on the page) is cleared by the table; the row is listed as contested instead.

rows.term: Kief and Chernigof (Governments of), кіевской и черниговской губ.
rows.reasoning: Both governments lie in Little-Russia, which the table maps to Ukrainians; a bare government name takes the people of the region it belongs to, not the people of the empire. Afanasyev names the same two governments in Russian ("Въ кіевской и черниговской губ.", 1868 p.330).
rows.note: The pilot filed these as Russians by the context rule (Ralston is writing about Russian peasants). A reader may prefer that reading for the 1870s, or object that the modern border is being read back.
rows.pilot: leshy /peoples_regions/3 would change from Russians to Ukrainians. The Phase 1 flag on it is not in the v2 log, so no current flag changes.

rows.reasoning: The Kharkov Government was Sloboda Ukraine, and Afanasyev places the rusalka form there directly after a sentence about the Little Russians. Same rule as Kief and Chernigof.
rows.note: The pilot filed Kharkov as Russians in vampir (Phase 1) and as Ukrainians in rusalka; the table makes it Ukrainians in both. A reader may object as for Kief and Chernigof.
rows.pilot: rusalka /names/variants/2: the attribution flag is cleared by the table (the OCR part of the flag stands). vampir's Phase 1 Kharkov row is not in the v2 entry, so nothing changes there.

rows.reasoning: Ralston's Ruthenians are the East Slavs of Austrian Galicia and Hungary, whom the modern usage counts as Ukrainians; the region text keeps "Ruthenians".
rows.note: Some of these communities identify as Rusyns, a separate people, not as Ukrainians. The table chooses Ukrainians and says so.
rows.pilot: domovoi: the term was left unmapped in a note (ralston1872 p.122). A re-run would add a Ukrainians row; the entry is not re-run.

rows.reasoning: Ralston gives a tale's provenance as "From the Voroneje Government" (1873 p.178). Most of the government was Great Russian.
rows.note: The southern districts of Voronezh were largely Little-Russian (Ukrainian) settlement, and the page does not say which district the tale came from, so a reader may file it as Ukrainians.
rows.pilot: No pilot entry uses the term; nothing changes.

rows.reasoning: "На Руси есть сказка про Лихо одноглазое" (1868 p.698) introduces the tale that Afanasyev then sets against a "малорусскій варіантъ" (p.699) and calls "великорусской сказкѣ" (p.700), so here Rus' is the Great Russian tradition. On 1869 p.549 ("На Руси думаютъ, что колдунъ ... можетъ ... сдѣлать его оборотнемъ") the next sentence turns to "На Украйнѣ и въ Бѣлоруссіи", which may be a contrast (Great Russians) or a narrowing of a statement about all the East Slavs.
rows.note: Rus' can name all the East Slavs. On 1868 pp.698-700 the pages set it against a Little-Russian form, which settles Russians there; on 1869 p.549 the page does not settle it, so the row is contested and a reader may take it as East Slavs in general.
rows.pilot: No pilot entry uses the term; nothing changes.

rows.term: великорусскій, великорусской ("Great Russian"), Great-Russian, великорусскіе, Великорусская, Great-Russia, великоруссы, великорусскихъ, великорусскимъ, великорусскими, великорусскія
rows.reasoning: Named directly: "Какъ въ великорусской сказкѣ" (1868 p.700). Great Russian is the 19th-century name for the Russians as distinct from the Little- and White-Russians. Ralston prints "The Great-Russian volkodlak becomes, says Afanasief, in Little-Russian vovkulak" (1872 p.404; the OCR reads "volTcodldlc"); Afanasyev has "великорусскіе поселяне" (1869 p.532) and "Великорусская редакція этой сказки" (1869 p.393).
rows.note: None.
rows.pilot: No pilot entry uses the term; nothing changes.

rows.reasoning: "сербской и словенской вилы" (1869 p.182) pairs the word with the Serbian vila, which reads as a second named people, the Slovenes, among whom the vila is attested.
rows.note: In 19th-century Russian "словенскій" can also mean Slavonic in general, which is no people; the page does not settle which Afanasyev means.
rows.pilot: No pilot entry uses the term; nothing changes.

rows.reasoning: Ralston cites "one of the Songs of Montenegro" (1873 p.205, footnote); the songs are those of the Montenegrins.
rows.note: A new people value. In the 19th century the Montenegrins were commonly counted as Serbs, and the songs belong to the Serbian epic tradition, so a reader may prefer Serbs.
rows.pilot: No pilot entry uses the term; nothing changes.

rows.reasoning: Ralston lists word forms by language ("vukodlak in Dalmatian vakudluk, in Bulgarian vrkodlak", 1872 p.404); the Slavic speech of Dalmatia is Croatian.
rows.note: Dalmatia's Slavs included Orthodox Serbs, and 19th-century writers often counted Dalmatian speech as Serbian, so a reader may prefer Serbs. The region text keeps "Dalmatia".
rows.pilot: No pilot entry uses the term; nothing changes.

rows.reasoning: "The Slavs in Istria believe that every single family has its own Vukodlak" (Machal p.229); the Slavs of Istria were mostly Croats, and Machal gives the Croatian form Krsnik first.
rows.note: The page names no people. Istria's Slavs were Croats and, in the north, Slovenes, and Machal also gives the Slovene form Kresnik, so a reader may file it as Slovenes or as both.
rows.pilot: No pilot entry uses the term; nothing changes.

rows.reasoning: Ralston pairs Galicia with Little-Russia for the Mavki (1872 p.142), and Afanasyev's Galician rusalki on the mountains are the same beings (1869 p.124); the Slavs of eastern Galicia were the Ruthenians, whom the table maps to Ukrainians.
rows.note: Western Galicia was Polish, and on 1868 p.343 ("Въ Польшѣ и Галиціи лисунки называются dziwożony") Afanasyev pairs it with Poland and gives a Polish name, so a reader may file that usage as Poles. The region text keeps "Galicia".
rows.pilot: rusalka: the Galician mountain clause (afanasyev1869 p.124) has no people row and says so in a note; a re-run would add a contested Ukrainians row. The entry is not re-run.

rows.reasoning: Afanasyev cites "По разсказамъ гуцуловъ" for the wild women (1869 p.803, addenda to pp.343-4). The Hutsuls are highlanders of Galicia and Bukovina, among the people the table maps as Ruthenians to Ukrainians.
rows.note: Follows the Ruthenians row: some Hutsuls identify as a separate people or as Rusyns rather than Ukrainians. The table chooses Ukrainians and says so.
rows.pilot: No pilot entry uses the term; nothing changes.
